subject: Post-demo follow-up: TTFT targets and streaming cadence for FastRetail proof-of-concept
messages:
From: Diego Fernandez <diego@redwood.ai>
To: Caleb Morris <caleb@fastretail.ai>, Amira Khan <amira.k@fastretail.ai>
Cc: Aditya Rao <aditya@redwood.ai>, Laura Bennett <laura@redwood.ai>

Subject: Post-demo follow-up: TTFT targets and streaming cadence for FastRetail proof-of-concept

Hi Caleb / Amira,

Thanks again for taking the demo earlier — really appreciate the clear signals on where latency/streaming matter for checkout assistance and live agent augmentation. Per our call, I wanted to capture the performance requirements we heard and propose next steps so the POC scope is unambiguous. I attached a draft SLO matrix (FastRetail-SLO-matrix.xlsx) and a mutual action plan (FR-MAP-v1.2.pdf).

Summary of requirements (as we heard them)
- Workloads: short prompt assistant (checkout prompts, ~30–80 tokens) and multi-turn agent assist (context up to ~1k tokens)
- TTFT: p50 <= 80ms, p95 <= 200ms for the short prompt assistant during normal traffic (spiky windows allowed per SLA)
- Sustained throughput: 5k generated tokens/sec across the cluster during peak; concurrency target: 300 simultaneous user sessions
- Streaming: client needs streaming token-by-token or small chunks; preferred: WebSocket or SSE with chunk cadence <= 200ms under load so UI can render typing-like behavior
- Degradation tolerances: if dedicated capacity saturated, fall back to a higher-latency model variant with explicit signal to UI (graceful degrade)

Open questions we flagged on the call
1) Is p95 TTFT measured from request receipt at the gateway (including network hop) or from model invocation? We'll standardize on gateway-to-first-token unless you prefer otherwise.
2) Do you require strict per-request ordering guarantees across the WebSocket stream for multi-tool responses?
3) Are there peak burst patterns (minutes/hour cadence) that exceed the steady-state concurrency we listed?

Proposed next steps
- Can you confirm that the TTFT p95 baseline should be gateway-to-first-token? (Caleb)
- We'll run a focused bench with your sample prompts + typical session patterns. Laura will scope a technical deep-dive to validate kernel / batching choices and expected TTFT under your payloads.
- Target: technical deep-dive next week; engineering PoC to follow (2–3 weeks).

If that aligns, I'll loop in an SRE from our Dedicated team and schedule an hour with Laura to capture sample prompts and realistic concurrency traces.

Thanks,

Diego Fernandez

Diego —

Thanks for the clear recap and for putting the SLO doc together. A few quick clarifications from our side after syncing with Eng: 

- Gateway vs model measurement: gateway-to-first-token is ideal for our dashboard (we want to show end-to-end experience). We can also provide packet capture spans if needed.
- Ordering: yes, strict ordering across a single user WebSocket stream is required for the agent assist flows (we have downstream tools that rely on stable event sequences).
- Bursts: our busiest 10-minute windows can spike to ~600 concurrent sessions for flash sales, but average daily peak is closer to 300. Our budget target is to keep p95 under 300ms during those 10-min bursts; 200ms is preferred for normal peak.

On chunk cadence: the UX team really dislikes long pauses; if you can guarantee chunks at least every 200ms under nominal load and indicate when degraded, we're good.

We can do the deep-dive next Wednesday morning PST. I'll get session traces and a sample prompt corpus (short & long) uploaded by Monday.

-Caleb

From: Laura Bennett <laura@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Post-demo follow-up: TTFT targets and streaming cadence for FastRetail proof-of-concept

Diego / Aditya —

Quick technical read on feasibility: the targets are achievable but will need tuned config and probably Dedicated capacity for consistent p95 under burst. Notes: 

- TTFT sources: network (gateway->edge), model warm vs cold (KV cache hit rate), and batching latency. For the short prompt assistant, keeping the KV cache warm and limiting batch window to <=5ms will keep p50 tight; p95 requires either overprovisioned pool or prewarmed model workers dedicated to FastRetail during flash windows.
- Streaming cadence: WebSocket is preferred for lower overhead; Redwood runtime can emit partial tokens in two modes: token-stream (single-token chunks) or micro-chunk (4–8 tokens per chunk). Micro-chunking reduces headers/per-chunk overhead but will increase TTFT for the very first token by ~10–20ms depending on kernel path. Achievable cadence estimates (nominal load on Dedicated pool): token-stream avg cadence ~60–120ms; micro-chunk cadence ~150–250ms.
- Fallbacks: recommend a policy that falls back to a quantized variant that preserves token semantics but accepts higher latency (~400–600ms p95) during extreme overload, and surfaces a distinct client event so the UI can show "degraded" badge.

Action items for tech deep-dive:
1) Get representative prompt corpus + session timing from FastRetail (Caleb said he'll upload Monday).
2) Laura to run bench matrix: model variants (FP16, 4-bit quantized), chunk modes (token vs micro-chunk), batch windows (1ms/5ms/10ms), concurrency steps (100/300/600). Results will be added to the SLO matrix.
3) Identify Dedicated capacity sizing options and cost delta for guaranteed p95=200ms at 600 concurrency bursts.

I'll prepare a short bench plan and share before the deep-dive.

—Laura
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
laura@redwood.ai
